items.name: Aspirin
items.how: Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 → ↓ platelet thromboxane A₂ for the platelet's lifespan
hx: Reversibly inhibits COX-2 → ↓ platelet thromboxane A₂ for a few hours
Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, so the effect lasts the platelet's 7–10-day life.
Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 → ↑ endothelial prostacyclin for the vessel's lifespan
The antiplatelet effect comes from less thromboxane A₂, not more prostacyclin.
Blocks platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors → ↓ fibrinogen cross-linking
That's abciximab-type action; aspirin blocks thromboxane synthesis.
items.sewhy: Aspirin blocks COX-1, reducing stomach-protecting prostaglandins (dyspepsia, ulcers) and platelet thromboxane for the platelet's whole life (bleeding, bruising). Shunting arachidonic acid towards leukotrienes can trigger bronchospasm in sensitive asthmatics.

ci.why: Reye's syndrome (acute liver failure and encephalopathy)
x: Kawasaki disease (coronary aneurysms and fever)
Aspirin is actually used to treat Kawasaki disease; the under-16 risk is Reye's syndrome.
Early growth plate closure (short stature and joint pain)
No effect on growth plates; the risk is Reye's syndrome.
Stevens–Johnson syndrome (skin and mucosal sloughing)
Not the classic risk; it's avoided because of Reye's syndrome.

ci.c: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleeding
ci.why: Removes protective prostaglandins and impairs clotting
x: Raises gastric acid by stimulating H₂ receptors
It doesn't act on H₂ receptors; it removes protective prostaglandins and impairs platelets.
Kills protective gut bacteria and impairs clotting
No antibacterial effect; losing prostaglandins weakens mucosal defence.
Increases gastrin release and portal pressure
Neither: it strips prostaglandin protection and stops platelets plugging the bleed.

ci.why: Adds a platelet defect to a clotting defect
x: Destroys the factor VIII already present
It doesn't affect factor VIII; it adds a platelet defect.
Triggers inhibitor antibodies against clotting factors
Inhibitors come from factor replacement; aspirin adds a platelet defect.
Speeds fibrinolysis of fresh clots
Not fibrinolysis; it stops platelets aggregating.

ci.why: COX block diverts arachidonic acid to leukotrienes → bronchospasm
x: COX block raises airway thromboxane → bronchospasm
Thromboxane falls; arachidonic acid is shunted to leukotrienes.
Salicylate triggers IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation → bronchospasm
It isn't IgE-mediated; it's the leukotriene shunt.
COX block lowers airway cAMP, blunting β2 agonists → bronchospasm
Not the mechanism; leukotrienes rise when COX is blocked.

items.name: P2Y12 inhibitors

uses.t: ACS, as DAPT with aspirin for 12 months

items.how: Block the platelet ADP (P2Y12) receptor → ↓ platelet aggregation
hx: Block the platelet thrombin (PAR-1) receptor → ↓ platelet aggregation
That's vorapaxar; clopidogrel and ticagrelor block the ADP (P2Y12) receptor.
Stimulate the platelet ADP receptor → exhaust platelet granules
They block the receptor, so ADP can't activate platelets.
Block von Willebrand factor binding → ↓ platelet adhesion
Not vWF; they block ADP-driven aggregation.
items.sewhy: Blocking platelet ADP receptors prevents aggregation, so bleeding and bruising are the main risks; ticagrelor also raises adenosine, causing breathlessness and bradycardia.

ci.why: Stops platelets plugging the bleed
x: Dissolves the clot already formed
That's thrombolysis; P2Y12 blockers stop platelets plugging the bleed.
Lowers clotting factor levels
No effect on clotting factors; platelets can't aggregate.
Causes thrombocytopenia
Platelet numbers are normal; they just can't aggregate.

ci.why: Higher intracranial bleeding risk
x: Higher risk of another ischaemic stroke
The trial showed net harm from intracranial bleeding.
Poor absorption after a stroke
Absorption isn't the issue; brain bleeds are.
Interacts with the statins given after stroke
No such interaction; the concern is intracranial bleeding.

ci.why: Rebleeding risk
x: Seizure risk
The concern is the brain bleeding again.
Cerebral vasospasm
Not vasospasm; rebleeding.
Hydrocephalus
The risk is rebleeding.

ci.why: CYP2C19 inhibition stops clopidogrel being activated
x: CYP2C19 induction makes clopidogrel toxic
Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, so less active drug forms.
Raised gastric pH stops clopidogrel dissolving
Not about pH; clopidogrel is a prodrug that needs CYP2C19.
Omeprazole displaces clopidogrel from albumin
Not displacement; it blocks activation.

items.name: Warfarin
items.how: Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase → ↓ factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C, S)
hx: Blocks vitamin K absorption in the gut → ↓ factors II, VII, IX, X
Absorption is fine; it blocks vitamin K recycling (VKORC1).
Activates vitamin K epoxide reductase → ↓ factors V, VIII, XI, XII
It blocks VKOR, lowering factors II, VII, IX and X.
Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase → ↓ fibrinogen and platelet production
It lowers the vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X), not fibrinogen or platelets.
items.sewhy: Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, reducing clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (bleeding). Protein C falls first, so clotting can briefly increase (skin necrosis), and anything changing CYP2C9 or vitamin K intake shifts the INR.

ci.why: Teratogenic (nasal hypoplasia, bone stippling) and causes fetal bleeding; use LMWH
x: Teratogenic (limb shortening, ear defects); switch to a DOAC
Warfarin embryopathy is nasal hypoplasia and stippled bones, and DOACs are avoided too: use LMWH.
Not teratogenic, but causes maternal haemorrhage at delivery; switch at 36 weeks
It is teratogenic and causes fetal bleeding; switch to LMWH.
Raises maternal BP → pre-eclampsia; switch to labetalol
Not about BP; warfarin is teratogenic and causes fetal bleeding.

ci.why: Prevents clot formation at the bleed
x: Dissolves the clot that's stopping the bleed
That's thrombolysis; warfarin stops new clot forming.
Raises BP, extending the bleed
No BP effect; it stops clots forming at the bleed.
Destroys platelets at the bleeding site
Platelets are untouched; clotting factors fall.

ci.why: Already low clotting factors; INR unpredictable
x: Already high clotting factors; INR falsely low
Liver disease lowers clotting factors, so warfarin's effect is unpredictable.
Warfarin is hepatotoxic; INR rises from liver damage
Not hepatotoxic; the liver already makes too few clotting factors.
Bile salts are lacking, so warfarin isn't absorbed
Absorption isn't the issue; clotting factors are already low.

ci.why: Head injury bleeds; unstable INR
x: Hip fractures from bone thinning; unstable INR
The concern with falls is bleeding inside the head.
Warfarin causes the drowsiness behind the falls; INR too low
Warfarin doesn't cause drowsiness; falls risk head bleeds.
Postural hypotension; INR drops after each fall
Warfarin doesn't affect BP; falls risk head bleeds and missed doses destabilise the INR.

items.name: DOACs
items.how: Directly inhibit factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or thrombin (dabigatran)
hx: Directly inhibit factor VIIa (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or fibrinogen (dabigatran)
The xabans inhibit factor Xa; dabigatran inhibits thrombin.
Directly inhibit thrombin (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or factor Xa (dabigatran)
It's the other way round: the xabans block Xa, dabigatran blocks thrombin.
Directly block platelet factor Xa receptors (all DOACs), stopping aggregation
They're anticoagulants acting on clotting factors, not platelets.
items.sewhy: DOACs directly block factor Xa or thrombin, so bleeding is the main risk; dabigatran capsules contain tartaric acid, which causes dyspepsia.

ci.why: Less effective than warfarin → valve thrombosis
x: More effective than warfarin → bleeding into the valve ring
They were less effective, with more valve thrombosis (and bleeding).
Bind to the valve metal and leach it into the blood
No; trials showed valve thrombosis on DOACs.
Cause haemolysis around the valve
Not the issue; they don't prevent valve thrombosis well enough.

ci.why: Not studied; warfarin preferred
x: Worsen the stenosis; warfarin preferred
No effect on the valve; these patients weren't studied, so warfarin is used.
Cause valve calcification; aspirin preferred
No; they simply weren't studied in this group.
Speed up atrial clot formation; heparin preferred
They weren't studied in mitral stenosis, so warfarin is used.

ci.why: More arterial clots than with warfarin
x: More bleeding than with warfarin
The trials stopped because of more arterial clots (especially strokes).
Antibodies neutralise DOACs completely
Not neutralised; they're simply less protective than warfarin.
They falsely prolong the INR, so dosing fails
DOACs aren't monitored by INR; they caused more arterial clots.

ci.why: Renally cleared → accumulation and bleeding
x: Nephrotoxic → worsening renal failure
Not nephrotoxic; they build up and cause bleeding.
Dialysed out, so they stop working
The concern is accumulation and bleeding.
Hepatically cleared, so levels drop
They're partly renally cleared, so they accumulate.

ci.why: Cross the placenta; no safety data
x: Proven to cause limb defects
No proven pattern; they cross the placenta and lack safety data, so LMWH is used.
Don't cross the placenta, but cause maternal bleeding
They do cross the placenta.
Speed up labour
Not the reason; they cross the placenta and there's no safety data.

ci.why: Prevents clot formation at the bleed
x: Dissolves clots that have already formed
That's thrombolysis; DOACs stop new clot forming.
Damages platelets at the bleed
Platelets are spared; clotting factors are inhibited.
Raises BP, extending the bleed
No BP effect; it stops clots forming.

items.name: Heparins
items.how: Boost antithrombin: LMWH mainly against Xa; UFH against Xa and thrombin
hx: Boost antithrombin: UFH mainly against Xa; LMWH against Xa and thrombin
It's the reverse: long UFH chains bridge thrombin; LMWH acts mainly on Xa.
Bind vitamin K: LMWH lowers Xa synthesis; UFH lowers thrombin synthesis
They act at once through antithrombin, not on factor synthesis.
Activate plasminogen: LMWH dissolves fresh clot; UFH dissolves old clot
They stop clot growing; dissolving clot is thrombolysis.
items.sewhy: Heparin boosts antithrombin (bleeding); in HIT, antibodies against heparin–PF4 activate platelets, causing low platelets and clots. Heparin suppresses aldosterone (high potassium), and long-term use thins bone.

ci.why: Prevents haemostasis
x: Causes vessel wall necrosis
No; it stops clotting (haemostasis).
Raises the platelet count dangerously
It can lower platelets (HIT); the issue is impaired haemostasis.
Triggers fibrinolysis
Not fibrinolysis; it blocks clot formation.

ci.why: Antibodies to heparin–PF4 cause clots and low platelets
x: Antibodies to heparin–albumin cause bleeding and high platelets
HIT antibodies target heparin–PF4 and cause clots with low platelets.
Heparin directly destroys platelets in the spleen
It's antibody-driven platelet activation (clots), not splenic destruction.
Antithrombin gets used up, causing bleeding
HIT causes clots, through heparin–PF4 antibodies.

ci.why: Rebleeding
x: Cerebral vasospasm
The risk is rebleeding.
Seizures
The concern is rebleeding.
Brain oedema
The risk is rebleeding.

ci.why: LMWH accumulates; use UFH or reduce dose
x: LMWH is nephrotoxic; use warfarin instead
It isn't nephrotoxic; it accumulates, so use UFH or reduce the dose.
LMWH stops working; double the dose
It accumulates, so the dose must come down.
UFH accumulates; use LMWH instead
UFH is the safer one in renal failure; LMWH accumulates.

items.name: Thrombolytics
items.how: Convert plasminogen to plasmin → breaks down fibrin clot
hx: Convert plasmin to plasminogen → breaks down platelet plugs
They convert plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin.
Activate factor XIII → loosens fibrin cross-links
Factor XIII cross-links fibrin; thrombolytics make plasmin to digest it.
Convert fibrinogen to fibrin → seals the vessel
That's thrombin's job; thrombolytics dissolve fibrin.
items.sewhy: Thrombolytics activate plasmin, which breaks down all clots including protective ones, so bleeding (including intracranial) is the major risk; alteplase also raises bradykinin (angioedema).

ci.why: High risk of a new brain bleed
x: High risk of a new ischaemic stroke
Thrombolysis risks bleeding, not new ischaemia.
Scar tissue stops the drug reaching the clot
Not the reason; a new brain bleed is likely.
Seizures from the old haemorrhage
The danger is a new bleed.

ci.c: Ischaemic stroke in last 3 months (for MI), brain tumour or AVM
ci.why: Fragile vessels bleed
x: The tumour absorbs the drug
Not the reason; fragile vessels bleed.
The drug raises intracranial pressure
The concern is bleeding from fragile vessels.
Old infarcts calcify and embolise
No; fragile vessels bleed.

ci.c: Active internal bleeding, recent major surgery or trauma
ci.why: Dissolves the clots stopping the bleeding
x: Stops new platelets forming
It doesn't affect platelet production; it dissolves existing clots.
Raises BP at the bleeding site
No BP effect; it breaks down the clots sealing wounds.
Stops wounds healing by blocking collagen
Not collagen; it dissolves the clots that stop bleeding.

ci.why: Catastrophic bleeding into the dissection
x: Dissolves the intimal flap into an embolus
The flap isn't clot; bleeding into the dissection is the danger.
Raises BP, extending the tear
No BP effect; it causes catastrophic bleeding.
Clots the false lumen, blocking branch arteries
It dissolves clot; bleeding into the dissection is the risk.

ci.why: ↑ haemorrhagic transformation
x: ↑ clot propagation
High BP raises the risk of bleeding into the infarct.
↓ alteplase reaching the clot
Not the reason; bleeding risk rises.
↑ cerebral vasospasm
The risk is haemorrhagic transformation.

items.name: Tranexamic acid
items.how: Antifibrinolytic: blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin
hx: Procoagulant: activates factor X and thrombin
TXA doesn't make more clot; it stops clot being broken down.
Antifibrinolytic: converts plasmin back to plasminogen
It blocks plasminogen's lysine-binding sites on fibrin.
Platelet activator: releases ADP from platelets
No platelet effect; it's an antifibrinolytic.
items.sewhy: Tranexamic acid stops clot breakdown, so in rare cases it can promote thrombosis; it irritates the gut and can lower the seizure threshold at high doses.

ci.why: Stops the body breaking clots down → propagation
x: Dissolves the clot into an embolus
TXA does the opposite: it stops clots being broken down.
Raises the platelet count → new clots
No platelet effect; it blocks fibrinolysis.
Turns the clot into an infected thrombus
No; it stops fibrinolysis, so the clot grows.

ci.why: High doses can trigger seizures
x: Interacts with all antiepileptics
Not an interaction; high doses themselves can cause seizures.
Causes hyponatraemia that triggers seizures
Not through sodium; TXA itself can provoke seizures.
Clots cerebral veins, triggering seizures
The effect is direct, at high doses.

ci.why: Renally excreted
x: Hepatically cleared
TXA is renally excreted, so reduce the dose.
Nephrotoxic
Not nephrotoxic; it's renally excreted.
Forms kidney stones
No; it accumulates because it's renally excreted.

items.name: Oral iron
hx: Stimulates erythropoietin release from the kidney
Iron is raw material for haemoglobin; it doesn't raise EPO.
Replaces iron for DNA synthesis in red cell precursors
Iron goes into haem; DNA synthesis needs B12 and folate.
Binds hepcidin to release stored iron
It simply replaces iron; hepcidin actually blocks absorption.
items.sewhy: Unabsorbed iron irritates the gut (nausea, pain, changed bowel habit) and turns stools black.

ci.why: Adds to toxic iron deposits (liver, heart, pancreas)
x: Blocks HFE gene repair, worsening the mutation
Iron doesn't affect genes; it adds to toxic deposits.
Triggers haemolysis of overloaded red cells
Not haemolysis; extra iron deposits in organs.
Adds to toxic copper deposits (liver, brain, cornea)
Copper overload is Wilson's disease; haemochromatosis is iron.

ci.c: Anaemia not caused by iron deficiency (e.g. thalassaemia trait)
ci.why: Won't help and risks overload
x: Turns thalassaemia trait into sickle cell disease
Impossible; it won't help and may overload.
Causes haemolysis in thalassaemia
Not haemolysis; it adds iron that isn't needed.
Speeds red cell production too much
It won't help non-iron anaemia; overload is the risk.

ci.why: Chelation: separate doses by 2 h
x: Enzyme induction: double their doses
Iron binds them in the gut (chelation); separate the doses.
Iron toxicity: halve the iron dose
Not toxicity; they bind each other in the gut.
Hepatotoxicity: monitor liver tests
Not liver toxicity; they bind each other in the gut.

items.name: Folic acid

uses.t: Pre-conception (400 μg; 5 mg if high risk)

items.how: Replaces folate for DNA synthesis in dividing cells
hx: Replaces folate for myelin synthesis in nerves
Myelin depends on B12; folate supports DNA synthesis.
Stimulates erythropoietin to boost red cell production
It's a building block for DNA, not an EPO stimulant.
Replaces folate for haem synthesis in red cells
Haem needs iron; folate is for DNA synthesis.
items.sewhy: Folic acid is a water-soluble vitamin with very few side effects; the main caution is that it can mask B12 deficiency.

ci.why: Corrects the anaemia while nerve damage (subacute combined degeneration) progresses
x: Worsens the anaemia while protecting the nerves
The reverse: it corrects the anaemia while nerve damage progresses.
Triggers an allergic reaction to intrinsic factor antibodies
Not allergy; it masks B12 deficiency while the nerves degenerate.
Blocks B12 absorption in the terminal ileum, causing pernicious anaemia
It doesn't block absorption; it hides the anaemia while nerves suffer.
